w11-ICS-L2-6.q:
The events A, B and C are mutually exclusive and exhaustive. P(A) = 0.45 and P(B) = 4 × P(C).
Find P(A ∪ B).
w11-ICS-L2-6.sol: Exhaustive and mutually exclusive, so P(A) + P(B) + P(C) = 1. 0.45 + 4 P(C) + P(C) = 1, so 5 P(C) = 0.55 and P(C) = 0.11. P(B) = 4 × 0.11 = 0.44. P(A ∪ B) = 0.45 + 0.44 = 0.89.

w11-ICS-L2-7.q:

The events A and B are such that P(A) = 0.8, P(B) = 0.4 and P(A ∪ B) = 0.88.
Determine whether A and B are independent. Answer yes or no.
w11-ICS-L2-7.sol: P(A ∩ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∪ B) = 0.8 + 0.4 − 0.88 = 0.32. P(A) × P(B) = 0.8 × 0.4 = 0.32. These are equal, so A and B are independent.

w12-ICS-L3-1.q:
In a group of 50 pupils, 28 play football (F), 25 play cricket (C) and 12 play both sports.
Find the probability that a pupil chosen at random plays neither sport.
w12-ICS-L3-1.sol: Venn diagram: both = 12, F only = 16, C only = 13, neither = 9. (Neither = 50 − (28 + 25 − 12) = 9.) Probability = 9/50.

w12-ICS-L3-4.q:
Of 80 students: 31 attend the art club (A), 34 attend the coding club (C) and 24 attend the science club (S). 9 attend A and C, 8 attend A and S, 12 attend C and S, and 6 attend all three.
Find the probability that a student chosen at random attends exactly one club.
w12-ICS-L3-4.sol: Work from the centre: all three = 6; A and C only = 9 − 6 = 3; A and S only = 8 − 6 = 2; C and S only = 12 − 6 = 6. A only = 20, C only = 19, S only = 10, none = 14. Favourable = 49, so P = 49/80.
